#1134. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

FIFA confirmed its plans to stage the 2031 Women's World Cup in North America, with the joint bid from the U.S., Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica officially getting the green light at an extraordinary FIFA Congress in Zurich on Monday.

The announcement comes a year after the co-hosts formalized their commitment to put in a bid, one that was ultimately the only contender for the 2031 tournament. Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica are all first-time hosts of the women's tournament, their inclusion in the bid part of an effort to accelerate the growth of women's soccer across the region. The 2031 World Cup, though, will also be another opportunity to showcase the growth of the women's game -- the U.S. has long been a hotbed for the sport, but its embrace of women's soccer has only grown since 2003, particularly with the increasing popularity of the uber-successful U.S. women's national team and the professionalization of the NWSL.

FIFA will return to the U.S. and Mexico fairly quickly after the two countries, alongside Canada, hosted the men's World Cup earlier this year, an experience that will prove to be relevant to the 2031 organizers from a logistical standpoint. Just as the men's World Cup did in 2026, the women's tournament will expand to 48 teams in 2031, a choice that ultimately resulted in the creation of a new competition footprint. U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone said last year that the expansion was the main impetus for including Costa Rica and Jamaica in a bid that was once envisioned as a 32-team competition in just the U.S. and Mexico.

"As soon as I knew for sure that was in the works, I went to [Concacaf] president Victor Montagliani and talked to him about our vision and that we wanted to make it bigger and include more countries throughout Concacaf and wanted to work with him to pick which countries would be best suited," Parlow Cone said at the time. "Obviously, quality of teams, stadiums, infrastructure. Outside of stadiums, like hotels, training facilities also went into the decision."

Monday's announcement officially kicks off the process for a tournament FIFA hopes will attract more than 4.5 million spectators and estimates will generate more than $4 billion in revenue, which would make it the highest revenue-generating women's sporting event in history.

FIFA's bid evaluation report lists 20 stadiums that could host games, though the actual bid includes more than 30 cities and 45 venues that will vie for the chance to host games in 2031. Most of the 14 cities across the U.S. and Mexico that hosted the 2026 tournament are back in the mix, including the host of this year's final, MetLife Stadium in the New York area, and the semifinal venues of AT&T Stadium in the Dallas suburbs and Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium. A few cities that did not make the cut last time around, though, are also interested -- Denver's Empower Field is on the list, as is the under-construction stadium in Washington, D.C., that the NFL's Washington Commanders will call home and is expected to be complete in 2030.

The list of contenders in Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica is understandably smaller considering each country's size and the resources available. While competition to host games could heat up around North America, a fairly straightforward answer is expected in Jamaica. The under-renovation Independence Park in the capital city of Kingston is the only venue listed in the bid.

The 2031 bid is attracting more interest from potential host cities than the 2026 tournament did for one reason in particular -- tournament organizers are inviting bids from a wider range of stadiums this time around.

This year's men's World Cup was hosted exclusively in NFL stadiums or similarly sized venues in Canada and Mexico, some of which will likely stage games again in 2031 and welcome the teams that are expected to draw big audiences like the host teams in their home countries. There are a number of venues with a capacity of 40,000 seats or fewer, like Geodis Park in Nashville, Tenn., and San Diego's Snapdragon Stadium, that could make the cut in the end. Tournament organizers are entertaining the idea that strong atmospheres in smaller stadiums might be preferable to half-full venues for games that are not expected to welcome large audiences, though a final decision has yet to be made.

The vast majority of games are likely to be staged in the U.S., just as they were for the men's World Cup this year.

There is little concern about North America's ability to host the Women's World Cup as far as the economics go. The U.S. alone is as ideal a market as any for a women's sporting event and has been for decades -- around 14 million people in the U.S. watched the national team beat China in the final via an iconic penalty shootout in 1999, while that tournament generated a $4 million profit on its $30 million operating costs. The question for 2031, though, is who will actually make money.

The U.S. cities that hosted the men's World Cup this year spent the months before and after the tournament complaining about the economics, the local host committees footing bills that reportedly ran as high as $150 million per city to actually stage the tournament. The host committees at times successfully lobbied the Trump administration for federal funding, but they continued to express concerns about the division of costs between the cities and FIFA. The host committees were also reportedly waiting for a further $1 million weeks after the World Cup ended despite a pledge from FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Potential host cities for the 2031 World Cup will likely advocate for a different split of the costs this time around, and the same could be true for the U.K.-set 2035 tournament. Local officials in the U.S. are reportedly contemplating banding together with the support of U.S. Soccer in the hopes of negotiating more favorable contracts with FIFA and avoiding fierce competition between the host cities that would strengthen FIFA's negotiating position.

#1132. Washington Spirit part ways with Adrian Gonzalez after loss in NWSL Championship

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Washington Spirit parted ways with head coach Adrian Gonzalez on Monday, less than 48 hours after a 2-1 loss to the Kansas City Current that marked the team's third successive defeat in the NWSL Championship.

Gonzalez was an assistant on the 2024 team that lost to the Orlando Pride in the final but he served as the interim before Jonatan Giraldez's midseason arrival from Barcelona. He then succeeded Giraldez after he left for France's OL Lyonnes, another club in Spirit owner Michele Kang's portfolio, midway through the 2025 campaign. He was a finalist for the NWSL's coach of the year award last season and maintained a consistency that has been a trademark for the Spirit in recent years, ensuring they continued to be serial contenders for titles under both Giraldez and Gonzalez.

For all their ambition, though, the Spirit have struggled to win major titles in the years since Kang took over the club in 2022. Their only title since is the 2025 Challenge Cup, a one-off game against the Pride, and have failed to win the NWSL Shield despite inching close on a handful of occasions while also falling short in the NWSL Championship games. They also failed to win the Concacaf W Champions Cup earlier this year, losing 5-3 to Club America in the final.

"I'm incredibly proud of what we've accomplished together at the Washington Spirit and grateful to the players, staff, ownership and supporters for their commitment and support throughout my time here," Gonzalez said in a club statement. "It has been an honor to lead this group, and I'm especially proud of the resilience and character the team has shown. A special thank you to the Spirit fans, who make this club truly unique. The connection and bond we've built with you has meant so much to me and made my time here even more special. Your passion and support are something I will always remember. While this chapter comes to an end, I'm excited for what lies ahead for the club and wish everyone continued success."

Gonzalez's departure also comes after Haley Carter became the president of soccer operations in the build-up to the 2026 season. Carter was previously with the Orlando Pride, who won both the NWSL Shield and NWSL Championship in 2024 after years of being a bottom-dweller in the league.

"We are grateful to Adrian for his leadership and the success he has helped bring to the Spirit over the past three seasons," Carter said in a statement. "He has led the team with class and professionalism and made a lasting contribution to this club. As we plan for the Spirit's future, all parties believe a change in leadership is necessary to build on that success and achieve our long-term sporting goals."

The search for Gonzalez's successor is underway and is likely to center around the Spirit's continuing quest to win the NWSL's top titles.

Since Kang's 2022 takeover, the ambitions of the Spirit have been clear as day. This is a team that is purpose-built to compete for titles, to the point that their attempts to keep Trinity Rodman in the NWSL led the league to create a brand-new rule and a historic contract for the player herself. The Spirit's entire roster, though, is impressive in its own right – Rodman counts Italy international Sofia Cantore amongst her partners in attack, while Tanzania's Clare Luvanga has scored four goals and notched three assists since her September arrival.

Gonzalez understood the assignment, even if the only accolade he walked away with was the 2025 Challenge Cup. He actually leaves the Spirit with 32 wins from 58 and a 1.84 points-per-game record, the best tally from a coach in the history of the NWSL. The strike on his record is that the Spirit did not rise to the occasion in the championship both last year and especially on Saturday, when a physical Current disrupted the momentum of the game and rattled the Spirit from start to finish. His will be a tough act to follow, though – he was able to get the best out of the players despite the stop-start nature of his responsibilities in the early stretch of his tenure and only confirmed that the Spirit are a club with high standards.

Considering the ambitions of the club, the coaching search will be an intriguing one. The Spirit are an attack-minded team and it would not be a surprise if a coach of that ilk lands the job, but Gonzalez's successor will ultimately be tasked with actually winning the titles that have eluded the club in recent years. Someone with a winning track record might be preferred and even if there are few obvious candidates, the Spirit likely have the pull – and the resources – to sign almost anyone they would like. It is not the only layer of uncertainty as the search begins – Carter has never hired a head coach during her years in NWSL front offices, joining the Pride after Seb Hines took the role and departing before his August departure.

#1130. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and said “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

Could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

So it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

#1129. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Could Real Madrid, Manchester City exploit PSG and Bayern woes?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Champions League's league phase enters its back half this week, but already you could be forgiven for looking further ahead. It is not so much that January will not provide some dramatic twists and turns, more that most of the contenders seem to have their affairs in order already. Yes, Bayern Munich have some work to do getting into the top eight, but most of the other sides from the top tier are in, well, the top tier.

Wednesday will bring a few of the big teams on the top-24 bubble to consider -- Atletico Madrid and Manchester United in particular have their feet a little closer to the fire than ideal -- but before then, let's keep our eyes fixed on the top of the table. Back-to-back winners Paris Saint-Germain look to be in a better state in table terms than they usually are, but might trouble be awaiting both them and Bayern?

Every match streams live on Paramount+, your home for every Champions League game all season long, plus replays, highlights and studio coverage breaking down the race for the top eight. If you haven't signed up yet, now's the time.

Recent weeks have not been kind to at least two of the three leading contenders. We'll come to Arsenal's injury issues shortly -- crucially, they appear to be less severe than had initially been feared -- but these have been brutal weeks for Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain.

For the former, the headline news was the loss of Harry Kane until what he termed "the business end of the season," but that is only the start. Michael Olise is out of the game against Lille, having already been sidelined against Arsenal. Luis Diaz has played only nine times in the Bundesliga and Champions League. As for Jamal Musiala, well, things generally aren't going well when players' union FIFPRO is having words. There are few quality alternates in Vincent Kompany's squad. As Chuck Booth noted over the weekend, depth issues have held Bayern back in Champions Leagues gone by. Rarely have those issues been so pronounced so early in the season.

PSG do not want for quality backup, particularly in their front line. It is just that they would not have planned on leaning as heavily on it as they will have to now that Desire Doue has followed Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in suffering a major knee injury. Now, it is worth saying that Ousmane Dembele flanked by two of Ferran Torres, Maghnes Akliouche and Mika Godts could be very effective. However, for the time being at least, the benefit that Luis Enrique gets from his wholesale rotation in Ligue 1 is going to be, at best, significantly less pronounced. There are doubtless some prospects in the PSG academy who can take on extra minutes, but the value of Akliouche, Godts et al. eating domestic minutes drops when they also need to rock up in the games that count in the Champions League.

Now, of course, neither of these teams need to fear the worst. PSG top the league phase, and Bayern still have some gimme games (Slavia Prague, Manchester United) to get back up the standings. In the old group stage, perhaps Bayern would have paid the price for their early-season injuries. Instead, where the Champions League is concerned, they need only to focus on getting their guys back for February. No such prospects for PSG, but they still have those midfielders and those defenders. Your heart hardly bleeds.

If you are the field, though, this might be a year where a path opens up. The coming days might hint at who can claim it. Real Madrid have selection dilemmas of their own, but have won nine straight in La Liga and the Champions League. Yan Diomande and Arda Guler flanking Kylian Mbappe works exceptionally well. Those wingers make for a slightly more effective defensive unit, but wins over Roma and AEK Athens have pointed to a glass jaw that better teams might shatter. There is a similar question over Barcelona, whose ferocious pressing shatters lesser opponents but teeters dangerously when their passes per defensive action drift into double figures.

Liverpool? They may not have the engine room to control knockout ties. The most intriguing dark horse, at least for this week, might be Manchester City. Then again, aren't they always the most intriguing team right now? Certainly, in their domestic games, they are playing like a team expecting the worst from the Premier League disciplinary procedure, intent on taking itself out of the title race before the probable points deduction does it anyway. Their 1-1 draw with Fulham betrayed a team that has the quality to win but not the intensity.

Is that a tap you can switch on and off? After all, even if they are sent to the Championship or beyond, they could still embarrass England's footballing authority by qualifying for the Champions League as holders. Even at 85% capacity so far this season, they profile in the inner circle across Europe's top five leagues. There is a path for a team that wants to get it together. Is that City?

When David Raya made his way off the field clutching his left arm, anguish stretched across his face, you could be forgiven for thinking that that season was happening to Arsenal again. They have recruited high-quality backups in almost every position and probably would have a higher-grade reserve goalkeeper if it weren't such a hard sell to cover for the best in the world in his position. And so when Kepa Arrizabalaga entered the fray, hearts sank in the away end at St. James' Park.

They soared on Monday afternoon when Mikel Arteta confirmed that Raya would not need surgery and that initial tests "showed something much more encouraging" given the enormous pain the Spaniard seemed to be in. The No. 1 will be unavailable against Borussia Dortmund, but he has not been ruled out of Sunday's clash with Manchester City. It was against that opponent that Kepa's reputation was so soured, a horror show in the EFL Cup final in which he conceded both of the shots on target he faced.

Since then, he has started only three games: elimination by Southampton in the FA Cup, where he was just as bad, a dead rubber against Crystal Palace and an EFL Cup win at Ipswich. Though it was the goals he conceded that cost Arsenal at Wembley, his distribution came under just as intense a spotlight, his inability to navigate the Man City press stalling attacks at their starting point. Raya is a master of breaking teams with his passing. Since the start of the season, he leads all Premier League goalkeepers in line-breaking passes under pressure and in passes that break through three lines. Asking your backup to replicate Raya's range is borderline unreasonable. If a goalkeeper could pass that well, they wouldn't be warming the Arsenal bench.

Anyway, the primary job of a goalkeeper, even in 2026, is actually to keep the ball out of the net. And while Kepa hasn't done great at that lately, it is hardly like he has been playing in rhythm. When he is, the 32-year-old is absolutely fine. Good enough, in fact, that when Arsenal signed him in the summer of 2025, it was viewed as something of a coup. In his year with Bournemouth, Kepa had profiled as an above-average shot-stopper at volume, saving 71.3% of efforts he faced and conceding two fewer goals than the expected goals value of the shots he faced. It was the same in Kepa's final year as a regular starter with Chelsea, where he kept nine clean sheets in 29 games. There are weaknesses in Kepa's game beyond his passing. He does not particularly command his area when crosses come in, certainly not compared to Raya. He hardly flies off his line like his compatriot either, but it is worth reaffirming that the standard he is being held against is the man voted the best goalkeeper in the world by his fellow professionals. Kepa is not going to raise a team's ceiling like the man he will likely replace on Wednesday -- what a wasted endeavor this would be if Illan Meslier starts -- but put him behind the best shot-suppressing defense in the business over an extended period and he would probably be good enough to ensure that Arsenal's ambitions are not capped. It would appear, however, that we will not get a definitive answer on that for a while yet. That is no bad thing for Arteta and Arsenal.

#1128. Self-serving Scottish clubs were always going to ensure Craig Mulholland's youth football revolution was doomed to failure

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:01 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 24 November 2026

Given how quickly things have unravelled under Sebastien Pocognoli, serious questions are now being asked of those in power at the Scottish Football Association.

Ian Maxwell and Craig Mulholland, the chief executive and chief football officer who led the recruitment process, certainly talked a good game when Pocognoli was appointed.

However, when Mulholland took up his position in the summer, his remit was much broader than merely the appointment of a new head coach for the national team. He was tasked with trying to initiate a much-needed revamp of youth development throughout Scottish football.

Only a few months into the job, those plans have already hit the buffers due to resistance from clubs, despite the obvious need for more young Scottish players to play more first-team football.

The SFA had proposed including two Under-21 players starting in cup competitions and the same age group playing a minimum of 6 per cent of all available minutes across a season in league competition.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland has met resistance in his bid to shake up the game

When it immediately became clear that several clubs in Scotland weren’t keen on that, a new watered-down version was then put back on the table.

Now there have been reports that those plans might be booted even further into the long grass and possibly won’t even be voted on at all this season.

As is always the case, the self-serving interest from clubs in Scotland will always trump the need for national reform.

But that is only part of the story. What is also of serious concern is the lack of quality coaching afforded to players in academies across the country.

If that was to be addressed, clubs would perhaps feel more obliged to play more younger players if they were ready for first-team football.

It is a multi-faceted problem – and one which Mulholland is no closer to solving. Clubs are selfish and will serve their own needs, with no obligation to buy into any new proposals.

The SFA could stand firm and try to force some of these plans through as non-negotiable. A tough stance, albeit one that risks becoming messy.

But nobody should be naïve enough to believe that self-interest from the clubs is the root of all problems here. It is much, much deeper than that.

#1126. LA communities kick out Big Oil

After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

Leading Nashville SC to a record low of 25 goals conceded and tying Tony Meola's record for the most clean sheets in an MLS season with 16, Brian Schwake has taken home Goalkeeper of the Year honors by a landslide, beating out finalists Matt Turner and Roman Bürki. He also set club records for wins, penalty kick saves (three), save percentage (78.4%), and goals against average (0.76).

It's astounding that Eduard Lowen is playing soccer, considering what the few years have looked like for him. In March of this year, his wife Ilona died from brain cancer after they managed through her diagnosis, with Lowen taking time off from the game to support her and her family. He returned to MLS play in April, scoring in his first start of the season for St. Louis City SC, but then was traded to San Jose after the World Cup break. During that time with San Jose, he became an important part of their playoff run with one goal and three assists.

It's going to be tough in the playoffs for Griezmann to overcome the defense, but considering what he has already done with the squad, there's no reason why Orlando should be counted out with the Frenchman next to Justin Ellis.

En route to setting a points record with 77 points to win the Supporters' Shield, Nashville SC were also led by a record-setting defense that only let the ball into the back of the net 25 times in an entire campaign. That success was rewarded with all three finalists for Defender of the Year coming from Nashville, but it's their newest signing that took home the award. Joining from Norwegian club Fredrikstad ahead of the season, Woledzi didn't need much time to adjust, appearing in every regular-season match and helping Nashville build from the back to maintain possession. It was a team effort to tie the MLS clean sheet record with 17 during the season, so it's only natural for one of their defenders to get the honors this season.

#1123. Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

#1122. Man United Confidential: Carrington crash adds to Mauricio Pochettino's woes, as new boss set to cut players' days off... and why the wait goes on for coach Silvia Tuya

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 12:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:16 EST, 24 November 2026

As if having his first training session as Manchester United head coach sabotaged by a drone wasn’t dramatic enough, Mauricio Pochettino’s second day at work saw access to the club’s training base blocked by a serious road accident.

The collision between a vehicle and a cyclist on one of the two approaches to Carrington, where United’s players and staff are regularly seen driving through a security checkpoint, meant it was closed off for several hours on Friday while an ambulance and police cars attended the scene.

Greater Manchester Police say the cyclist was taken to hospital to receive treatment for injuries that were not life-threatening and no arrests were made.

However, anyone leaving Carrington had to take an alternative route in the opposite direction. That included the players after training and Pochettino and his staff following his first pre-match press conference.

The accident on Friday completed an eventful 48 hours at Carrington after a rogue drone operator filmed 12 minutes of Pochettino’s first training session and posted it on YouTube. He later took the video down and apologised for the intrusion, which United sources said was the right thing to do – even though they had not contacted the uploader directly and do not intend to take legal action against him.

They insisted there was not a breach of security at Carrington, but claimed a number of laws had been broken. Insiders promised a robust response to any further incidents to protect the rights of the club and its staff, and warned that those responsible would be ‘exposing themselves to significant legal and financial risk’.

It's been a testing first few days for Mauricio Pochettino as Manchester United boss

One of the unexpected issues to hamper the Argentine was a drone filming his first training session

Meanwhile, players leaving Carrington last Friday had to take an alternative route after a serious road accident near United's training ground

Confidential understands Pochettino ordered the United players into Carrington an hour early on Monday morning to flush the Liverpool defeat out of their systems as soon as possible.

The squad were pictured arriving around 8.30am as they looked to regroup after the 4-0 hammering at Anfield and begin their preparations for the Champions League tie against Sporting Lisbon in Portugal on Wednesday night.

The Argentine is eager to spend as much time as possible with the players on the training ground, having only taken over as United boss last Wednesday – four days before the Liverpool clash.

United now face 11 games in 43 days and sources believe there may not be too many days off as Pochettino tries to haul his team out of the relegation zone and ensure qualification for the knockout stage of the Champions League.

At least the indications are that he will allow the players to stay at home the night before games at Old Trafford, rather than having them cooped up in a hotel like some previous United managers.

Pochettino ordered the United players into Carrington an hour early on Monday morning to flush the Liverpool defeat out of their systems

Matheus Cunha won’t play any part against Sporting following his red card in United's last Champions League tie against Roma three weeks ago.

Confidential has learned the Brazilian was set to claim the player of the match award after scoring two late goals in the 3-2 win over Roma, only for UEFA to step in.

UEFA rules prevent a player who has been sent off from receiving the award and so the selector – in this case Steve Cooper, the former Leicester, Nottingham Forest and Swansea boss who is now one of the governing body's technical observers – was forced into a late switch, picking Bruno Fernandes instead.

Cunha’s absence will be keenly felt in Portugal. He played no part in Tuesday’s training session at Carrington, instead working on his own in the gym.

At a time when United have the most porous defence in Europe’s top five leagues and Matthijs de Ligt, Leny Yoro, Lisandro Martinez and Ayden Heaven are all struggling for form, Pochettino is going to need Harry Maguire.

Pochettino overlooked the experienced Englishman from the start for the trip to Anfield but ended the match with Maguire on the pitch and he was United’s best defender on another desperate afternoon.

Maguire is walking the tightrope of a ban as he remains on four yellow cards after 11 league games. Players are hit with a one-match ban once they receive five or more yellows prior to the conclusion of the 19th league game of the season – eight matches from now.

Even after Yoro's red card at Anfield was overturned on appeal, Pochettino can ill-afford to be without Maguire going forward.

Pochettino is going to need the experience of Harry Maguire to hold his defence together but he faces a ban if he is booked again

United are still waiting to see if Pochettino’s strength and conditioning specialist Silvia Tuya can join his staff at Carrington despite hiring new fitness coach Sam Wilson.

Wilson has joined United following his departure from Parma in October, having only moved to the Italian club as head of performance in the summer after 12 years at Arsenal.

It is understood Tuya has not yet been confirmed as part of Pochettino’s backroom team because she is waiting to see if a work permit will be approved.

She joined the US national team staff in October 2024 shortly after Pochettino, and travelled with him, first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino and analyst Alec Scott when they flew from Cincinnati to Manchester by private jet last week.

Strength and conditioning specialist Silvia Tuya has not yet been confirmed as part of Pochettino’s backroom team

Some of the early changes under Pochettino have been more subtle than others. Observant fans may have noticed that when the club announced the team to face Liverpool at 3.15pm on Sunday, it was in positional order.

Previously, United’s line-up has been listed numerically, leaving fans to deliberate over the formation. But Pochettino liked to name his team positionally at Tottenham and Chelsea, and admitted in a Q&A on MUTV last week that he wants to do the same at United.

It was clear from the club’s social media post on Sunday that Pochettino would be sticking to the 4-3-2-1 formation favoured by Michael Carrick, with Patrick Dorgu returning on the left wing and Cunha leading the attack.

Not that it lasted very long, as Pochettino admitted he was forced to put his game plan ‘in the bin’ inside eight minutes when Yoro was sent off.

This weekend’s match-up between United and Brentford brings together the most ill-disciplined English team in all competitions and the dirtiest team in the Premier League.

No English team has had more players sent off this season than United’s four – Yoro twice, Cunha against Roma and Martinez against Chelsea.

Meanwhile, Brentford are bottom of the Premier League’s disciplinary 'points table' thanks to their three red cards and 22 yellow cards. So expect referee Rob Jones to be a busy man on Pochettino’s home debut.

Leny Yoro brings down Alexander Isak at Anfield and is sent off - his second red card of the season

Richard Arnold, who preceded Omar Berrada as United's chief executive, pocketed a £5.53m pay-off to stand down after Ineos moved into the club

While Omar Berrada found himself back in the firing line last weekend, the man he succeeded as United’s chief executive was cutting a much more relaxed figure.

Richard Arnold, who led United between February 2022 and December 2023, was spotted enjoying himself on Chester’s popular Eastgate Street on Saturday night – 24 hours before a beleaguered Berrada watched United’s 4-0 thrashing 30 miles down the road at Anfield.

After stepping up to replace Ed Woodward, Arnold was in charge of United for the period spanning United’s strategic review which led to Sir Jim Ratcliffe acquiring 29 per cent of the club. Once it became clear that Ineos would take over the day-to-day running of United, he accepted a £5.53million pay-off to stand down, with the club’s general counsel Patrick Stewart stepping in on an interim basis.

Arnold is now enjoying a quieter life as an executive director at Norton Motorcycles and, it would appear, nights out close to his home near Chester.

It was there that he met a group of United protesters outside his local pub in June 2022 and admitted that the last 12 months had been ‘a f****** nightmare’ and United had ‘f****** burned through cash’. Nothing much seems to have changed since then.

#1120. Premier League x Stonewall partnership ends, new LGBTQ+ campaign to be launched

The Premier League is set to introduce a new LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, launched in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences."

Despite Stonewall's efforts, recent reports from Kick It Out reveal an alarming increase in discriminatory incidents in football, including rises in sexism, transphobia and faith-based abuse, with racism continuing to be the most prevalent issue.

Controversies around playersâ attitudes to rainbow armbands have also made headlines. Last season, Ipswich captain Sam Morsy declined to wear one due to religious beliefs, while Crystal Palaceâs Marc GuÃ©hi faced criticism for personalising his armband with the phrase âI Love Jesus.â

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped plans for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players currently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

Details of the Premier Leagueâs new campaign are still under wraps, but as the league presses âreset,â thereâs hope it will introduce a meaningful and effective initiative that advances equality rather than undermines it.

Double change for Liverpool as Isak and Mac Allister replace Ngumoha and Nyoni.

Huge double block from Chelsea and how have Liverpool not scored? Tsimikas’ cross to the back post is headed back across the six-yard box to find Wirtz, who you think is going to score but Colwill makes the block. Then Barcola has a shot blocked by Acheampong.

It is full time at both Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light, where Crystal Palace and Sunderland have booked their places in the League Cup quarter-finals.

Tsimikas gives it away inside his own half and Chelsea counter. Neto drives inside and finds Rogers, who skips past Gomez. Rogers then finds the overlapping Palestra on the left side of the box and the Italian is denied by Mamardashvili at his near post.

Manchester City have just beaten Brighton 4-3 on penalties whilst on the south coast Bournemouth have comfortably beaten Aston Villa 3-0. Both sides are into the hat for tonight’s quarter-final draw.

Lavia cynically brings down Ngumoha as the Liverpool forward drove through the Chelsea half and is correctly booked.

Liverpool are taking off Van Dijk and Jacquet is coming on in his place. No injury for Van Dijk.

What a terrific cup tie this has been. It helps when there is an edge between the sides and you can feel the tension in the air. What has been noticeable in the last three games at Anfield, though, is the change in the atmosphere. Slowly but surely the locals are buying into what Andoni Iraola is trying to achieve. Liverpool could lose this game tonight by going all out to win it but there is a clearly identity developing that makes you think they are starting to get on the right lines.

After Gakpo fouls Lavia, Chelsea have a free-kick just over 25 yards out. Rogers lines it up but his effort is terrible, flying into The Kop.

Chelsea are going to make a triple change. Palestra, Barco and Emegha come on, with the latter on for his Chelsea debut. Gusto, Caicedo and Welbeck head off.

Good save from Penders. The ball comes to Barcola outside the Chelsea penalty area. The Frenchman drives inside before getting his shot away from the edge of the box. The shot takes a small deflection and Penders does well to make the save down to his left.

The game between Manchester City and Brighton at The Etihad has ended 2-2, therefore it has now gone to penalties.

Chances at both ends. Gomez whips in a cross from the right and picks out Araujo in the centre of the box but the Uruguayan’s powerful header is straight at Penders. He probably should have scored.

Then Chelsea counter and Rogers is in acres of space. His shot from just outside the box takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner, which comes to nothing.

Gusto’s behaviour in recent minutes has been appalling. First he went down after virtually no contact from Van Dijk and now goes down again, once more not a foul. He shows his boot to the linesman as if it came off in a challenge from Barcola but the replays show that his boot did not come off and he was attempting to con the officials.

Andoni Iraola is turning to his bench for the first time tonight and makes a double substitution as Wirtz and Barcola replace McConnell and Koumas. Some double change that for Liverpool!

Fascinating to watchg Trey Nyoni and the responsibility he has taken on his shoulders. He’s only 19 but those who have worked with him since he arrived at Liverpool as a 16-year-old will tell you he has a maturity of someone in their mid-twenties. He has tried to get on the ball and play, he’s been strong when it’s been required and always been in the right place to get a foot in. He’s going to play a lot of games for Liverpool if he maintains this trajectory.

Achemapong scythes Ngumoha down as the latter cut inside and the former is correctly booked.

Down on the south coast, Bournemouth appear to be cruising into the quarter-finals as Alvaro Rodriguez has put them 3-0 up against Aston Villa.

Should Rogers have done better there? In fortuitous circumstances, he is played through but he does not show the conviction to drive towards the Liverpool penalty area. His touch lets him and the ball rolls through to Mamardashvili.

Moments later, Rogers forces Mamadrashvili into a save to his left and the Liverpool players are furious that a handball was not given. It clearly hit Rogers’ arm before he shot but Chelsea do have the corner. Chelsea play it short before eventually Henderson swings it in before Araujo heads away.

We are back under way at Anfield. No changes from either side at the break.

Manchester City have equalised at home against Brighton, with Rayan Cherki’s free-kick from just outside the box taking a big deflection off his teammate Vitor Reis and ending up in the back ot the Brighton net.

Manchester City 1 Brighton 2 (70’)Bournemouth 2 Aston Villa 0 (58’)Fulham 0 Crystal Palace 1 (56’)Sunderland 3 Brentford 1 (56’)Liverpool 1 Chelsea 1 HT

Bournemouth have doubled their advantage against Aston Villa through Lewis Cook just over five minutes into the second half.

Possession: Liverpool 50%-50% ChelseaShots: 6-2Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 5-0Touches in opposition box: 5-9

The first half is brought to an end at Anfield and the game is level at 1-1 going into the break. Rogers put Chelsea in front from the spot only for Gakpo to also score a penalty moments later to equalise for Liverpool.

The outswinging corner is sent in from the left but Araujo’s header goes over the bar. Meanwhile, Lacroix is slowly limping his way around the pitch to the tunnel and is moving very gingerly, which could suggest an extended period on the sidelines.

As we enter three minutes of added time, Colwill replaces the injured Lacroix.

Liverpool can sense a second goal. First, Gakpo has a shot saved by Penders before Ngumoha wins the hosts a corner. Before that is taken, play has been stopped as Lacroix is down clutching at his left hamstring.

Not a murmur from Xabi Alonso as his side take the lead. The penalty Morgan Rogers dispatched went in the same corner as Alonso picked in the 2007 Champions League semi-final and perhaps he had a sense of what was coming as Liverpool are now level and it’s a fair reflection of how an intriguing opening 45 minutes has played out. It really wouldn’t be a surprise if we need spot-kicks to separate these teams at 90 minutes.

Like Rogers moments ago, Gakpo sends the goalkeeper the wrong way and puts the penalty away to equalise. Gakpo slots into the bottom left corner in front of The Kop and the Dutchman continues his fine scoring record in this competition. Both sides have been gifted penalties and both teams take advantage.

Cody Gakpo slots home a penalty to equalise for Liverpool against Chelsea! 💪 https://t.co/rS775LH0Gb

Like London buses, two penalties come in quick succession. From a Liverpool corner out on the left, Fofana is penalised for a handball and the referee has no choice but to point to the spot. The Chelsea players protest but it clearly hit Fofana’s arm, which was above his head.

Rogers sends Mamardashvili the wrong way and puts Chelsea 1-0 up in front of their travelling supporters. It was a quality penalty from Rogers, who deposited it into the right corner of the goal. It is a gift for Chelsea, who did not look like scoring but are gifted a chance to score through that silly Gravenberch challenge.

Morgan Rogers puts Chelsea in front against Liverpool from the spot! 🎯 https://t.co/ocMXFNCW9F

Caicedo goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area and the referee points to the spot. It is a silly and needless challenge from Gravenberch, who slides into the back of Caicedo and gives the referee no choice but to give a penalty. Not that it would be overturned but there is no VAR anyway.

Ex-Liverpool man Henderson was holding the ball for a while but now hands over to Rogers to take...

They are into the second half at Manchester and Brighton have retaken the lead through Georginio Rutter. Brighton now lead Manchester City 2-1.

That is a gift from Chelsea. The communication at the back between Gusto and Fofana is poor, with the former playing a poor pass backwards looking for Fofana, who cannot reach it and the ball rolls behind for the easiest of corners for Liverpool in front of The Kop.

Gakpo takes an outswinging corner but Welbeck is on hand to head away at the front post.

We are yet to see the first goal of the night at Anfield but they are flying in at the Stadium of Light. Brentford have pulled a goal back against Sunderland through Callum Wilson and it is now 3-1 in the north east.

Chelsea want a penalty. Rogers goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area under a challenge from Araujo but it was a fair shoulder-to-shoulder challenge and that is not a penalty.

At the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in dreamland. Malick Fofana has put them 3-0 up against Brentford closing in on half-time.

A wasted free kick from Chelsea, and goodness, Austin McPhee is not happy. Chelsea’s set piece coach was up on the touchline, remonstrating to nobody in particular but it was obvious to see the frustration that the plan he has worked on - a chip to the side, a cutback into the middle - has fallen down at the first attempt. To compound his fury, McPhee just blew a gasket after Chelsea were not awarded a penalty following a coming together between Ronald Araujo and Morgan Rogers.

Tsimikas has let Ngumoha down there. Ngumoha does brilliantly to dribble through two Chelsea defenders around the halfway line and drives down the left. He then plays the ball outside to Tsimikas, who should do so much better with his cross but picks out the front-post defender Lacroix.

Meanwhile at Craven Cottage, Crystal Palace have taken the lead at Fulham thanks to Eddie Nketiah.

McConnell becomes the second Liverpool player to be booked tonight for handball. He lost the ball on halfway and cynically handled the ball as Rogers attempted to counter. A fairly clear-cut booking for McConnell there.

A reminder that there is no VAR tonight and if the game is level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. Referee Darren England has summoned Chelsea captain Caicedo and former Liverpool midfielder Henderson over for a word.

Caicedo puts Tsimikas’ cross from the left behind for the first corner of the night. Gakpo sends in the inswinger but the whistle goes as Chelsea are awarded a free-kick for a foul from Tsimikas on Gusto.

There has yet to be a goal at Anfield but at the Stadium of Light Sunderland have doubled their lead over Brentford courtesy of Tymur Tutierov’s goal.

The first booking of the night at Anfield goes the way of the home side. Koumas slides in to try and block a clearance from Lacroix and is booked. Koumas barely touched Lacroix and that is never a yellow card.

Meanwhile, in the north east, Sunderland have taken the lead against Brentford through Chemsdine Talbi.

Brighton had led in Manchester but the home side have just equalised. Mateo Kovacic has scored from range to bring Manchester City level with five minutes to go in the first half.

Clear to see in these early exchanges that Cody Gakpo has been deployed as Liverpool’s main “striker” with Lewis Koumas, James McConnell - who played in the 2024 final when Liverpool beat Chelsea 1-0 - and Rio Ngumoha operating in behind him. Jordan Henderson seems to be the man whom Xabi Alonso wants to trigger Chelsea’s press. They are playing a rigid 4-5-1 formation but, this being Alonso, the system is always flexible. His ethos is to be able to play two or three systems in a game if needed.

Ngumoha drives at Neto down Liverpool’s left and is felled by the Portuguese forward. It is an obvious free-kick and Neto is a touch fortunate not to be booked for that blatant foul. Ngumoha, who was fantastic for Liverpool against Villarreal in the Champions League just over a week ago, already into the action.

Tsimikas clips in the delivery but it is headed away by Lacroix.

The second goal in the League Cup this evening has come in Manchester and has gone the way of the away side. Malick Yalcouye has put Brighton in front against Manchester City on the half-hour mark.

We are under way at Anfield. Who will book their place in the League Cup quarter-finals; Liverpool or Chelsea?

Jordan Henderson is busily going around geeing up Chelsea’s players, in exactly the same fashion as he did when he played in this stadium for 12 years. He got an ovation here in May, when Brentford drew 1-1, that left him extremely emotional but it remains to be seen what will happen when he gets his first touch this evening. There has been no acknowledgement - yet - from The Kop and the same is true for Xabi Alonso. But, then again, why would there be when there is such lingering enmity between these clubs?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at Anfield. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Liverpool: Mamardashvili; Araujo, Gomez, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; McConnell, Nyoni; Ngumoha, Gravenberch, Gakpo; KoumasSubstitutes: Alisson, Endo, Jacquet, Wirtz, Isak, Mac Allister, Chiesa, Barcola, Chambers.

Chelsea: Penders; Acheampong, Lacroix, Fofana, Gusto, Caicedo, Lavia, Henderson, Neto, Welbeck, Rogers.Substitutes: Sharman-Lowe, Colwill, Subuloye, Palestra, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao, Quenda, Emegha.

Has come on the south coast, where Bournemouth have taken the lead against Aston Villa courtesy of Amine Adli’s goal inside the opening 10 minutes.

“The cups are important for us this year. For sure, we face today a good challenge, coming to Anfield, and we want to be in the next round. It is another competition. We know it is another format, it is make-or-break, so we want to make it happen today with a great performance.

“From the beginning we have taken it seriously. We have a tough game and we want to have a good feeling that we are competing. We have to do many great things. In one game there can be many little games with the energy created. These players have played here before. We have practiced penalties but sometimes it is about the feeling of the day.”

The games at the Vitality Stadium, Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light have just begun. That means four of the five ties tonight have started, with just the game at Anfield to begin in just over 10 minutes.

At The Etihad, Manchester City have kicked off against Brighton. Then, there are three 7.45pm kick-offs before Liverpool begin against Chelsea at Anfield at 8pm.

More than two years have passed since Rio Ngumoha chose to leave Chelsea for Liverpool, but the frustration remains at Stamford Bridge. The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It must sting to see a London boy, one of their own, now delighting the Anfield crowd.

For many at Chelsea, the anger at Ngumoha’s departure in 2024 will probably never subside. Or, at least, it will not subside while he continues to develop so thrillingly at Liverpool. Such was Chelsea’s annoyance at the time of his exit, Telegraph Sport reported last year, Liverpool’s scouts were subsequently banned from attending matches at their academy centre.

Liverpool: Mamardashvili; Araujo, Gomez, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; McConnell, Nyoni; Ngumoha, Gravenberch, Gakpo; KoumasSubstitutes: Alisson, Endo, Jacquet, Wirtz, Isak, Mac Allister, Chiesa, Barcola, Chambers.

Chelsea: Penders; Acheampong, Lacroix, Fofana, Gusto, Caicedo, Lavia, Henderson, Neto, Welbeck, Rogers.Substitutes: Sharman-Lowe, Colwill, Subuloye, Palestra, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao, Quenda, Emegha.

Xabi Alonso spent five years as a player at Anfield between 2004 and 2009. He has returned twice as an opposition manager, with both ending in defeats; one as Bayer Leverkusen boss and one as Real Madrid manager.

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.
